summary: We are testing whether NSGA-II's previously demonstrated convergence advantage over random search (91-eval gap on Qwen3-14B) transfers to a different model architecture (Llama-3.1-8B), and whether the magnitude of the advantage scales predictably with Pareto front density as explained by the KV stress interaction mechanism.
key_points: Four arms: (1) h-robustness characterizes Llama-3.1-8B's Pareto density via exhaustive enumeration (predicted 6-12% vs Qwen's 4.5%, driven by weaker KV stress from 32 vs 40 layers), (2) h-main runs NSGA-II on Llama expecting a smaller convergence gap of 40-70 evals (vs Qwen's 91) because higher density reduces random search's disadvantage, (3) h-control-negative confirms random search on Llama reaches 95% exhaustive HV within 200 evals, (4) h-ablation reproduces the Qwen3-14B rate=50 result in the same session to rule out infrastructure confounds.

Confirmation criteria: Llama Pareto density lands in 6-12%, NSGA-II convergence gap shrinks to 40-70 evals (portability confirmed but with predicted scaling), random search exceeds 95% HV at 200 evals, and Qwen ablation reproduces iter-5 gap within ±10 evals of 91.

Refutation signals: If Llama density is LOWER than 4.5% (different dominance structure from high throughput ceiling), if convergence gap is ≥91 evals (portability holds but scaling prediction wrong — possibly tp×instance allocation is the binding structure for smaller models), or if gap <30 evals (NSGA-II advantage becomes negligible at high density, suggesting a ~10-12% threshold).
